summary: Updates the IP Performance Metrics framework from RFC 2330 for IPv6 and IPv4-IPv6 coexistence. It extends standard-formed packets to include IPv6, deprecates the minimal IP packet definition, and augments the aspects that distinguish measurement types.

plainLanguage.summary: When you measure a network by sending test packets, the result depends on exactly what kind of packets you sent. This document brings the measurement framework up to date for IPv6 and says which details of a test packet must now be reported alongside the numbers.

questions: how does nat affect network measurements
subtitle: Brings IPv6 and IPv4-IPv6 translation into the IP Performance Metrics framework's idea of a standard-formed test packet.

tldr.problem: The framework for measuring network performance was written for IPv4 and never extended, even though its authors said it would need to be.
tldr.mechanism: The document updates the framework's definition of a standard-formed packet to cover IPv6, expands the list of packet characteristics that measurements must state, and retires an old definition that was never used.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 2330, so the framework used for Internet performance measurement now covers IPv6, and it identifies where translation, NAT and header compression make measurements harder.

facts.label: Deprecates
facts.value: The concept of the minimal IP packet from A to B

today: RFC 8468 is an Informational document that updates RFC 2330, so the IP Performance Metrics framework now covers IPv6 and IPv4-IPv6 coexistence alongside the original IPv4 material. It has no IANA actions, and it defers work on passive and hybrid measurement to future documents.

sections.title: Why the Framework Needed Updating
sections.content:
The IETF IP Performance Metrics working group first created a framework for metric development in RFC 2330. That framework has stood the test of time and enabled the development of many fundamental metrics. It has been updated in the area of metric composition and in several areas related to active stream measurement of modern networks with reactive properties.

The framework recognised that many aspects of an IP packet can influence its processing during transfer across the network. In Section 15 of RFC 2330, the notion of a standard-formed packet is defined, but the definition was never expanded to include IPv6, even though the authors of RFC 2330 explicitly identified the need for this update: the version field is 4, with the note that later the definition would be expanded to include 6. In particular, IPv6 Extension Headers and protocols that use IPv6 header compression are growing in use, and this memo provides the needed updates to the original definition.

The scope is to update key sections of RFC 2330, adding considerations that will aid the development of new measurement methodologies intended for today's IP networks. Specifically, it expands the Type-P examples in Section 13 of RFC 2330 and expands the definition of a standard-formed packet to include IPv6 header aspects and other features. Other topics that might be updated or augmented are deferred to future work, including passive measurement and the various forms of hybrid active and passive measurement.
sections.plainLanguage: The measurement framework dates from 1998 and was written for IPv4. Its own authors left a note saying it would need to be extended, and twenty years later it still had not been, so this document does the work.

sections.title: Packets of Type-P
sections.content:
A fundamental property of many Internet metrics is that the measured value depends on the characteristics of the IP packets used to make the measurement. Potential influencing factors include IP header fields and their values, as well as higher-layer protocol headers and their values. Consider an IP-connectivity metric: one obtains different results depending on whether one is interested in connectivity for packets destined for well-known TCP ports or unreserved UDP ports, those with invalid IPv4 checksums, or those with a TTL or Hop Limit of 16. In some circumstances these distinctions result in special treatment of packets in intermediate nodes and end systems, for example if Diffserv, Explicit Congestion Notification, Router Alert, Hop-by-Hop extensions or Flow Labels are used, or in the presence of firewalls or RSVP reservations.

Because of this distinction the document introduces the generic notion of a packet of Type-P, where in some contexts P is explicitly defined, for example exactly what type of packet is meant, partially defined, such as with a payload of B octets, or left generic. This allows a generic IP-Type-P-connectivity or a more specific IP-port-HTTP-connectivity. Whenever a metric's value depends on the type of packets involved, the metric's name will include either a specific type or a phrase such as Type-P, so an IP-connectivity metric is not defined but an IP-Type-P-connectivity metric and perhaps an IP-port-HTTP-connectivity metric. This naming convention is an important reminder to be conscious of the exact type of traffic being measured.

If the information constituting Type-P at the source is found to have changed at the destination, or at a measurement point in between, the modified values must be noted and reported with the results. Some modifications occur according to the conditions encountered in transit, such as congestion notification, or because of the requirements of segments of the source-to-destination path. For example, the packet length changes if IP headers are converted to the alternate version or address family, or if optional Extension Headers are added or removed. Even header fields that typically change in transit may be relevant to specific tests: Neighbor Discovery Protocol packets are transmitted with the Hop Limit value set to 255, and the validity test specifies that the Hop Limit must have a value of 255 at the receiver too, so for that test the correct Hop Limit value is of high relevance and must be part of the Type-P definition.

Local policies in intermediate nodes based on examination of IPv6 Extension Headers may affect measurement repeatability, though if intermediate nodes follow the recommendations for processing extension headers, repeatability may be improved to some degree.

A closely related note is that it would be very useful to know whether a given Internet component, such as a host, link or path, treats equally a class of different types of packets. If so, any one of those types can be used for subsequent measurement of the component, which suggests devising a metric or suite of metrics that attempts to determine that class. Load-balancing over parallel paths is one particular example where such a class is more complex to determine: load balancers and routers often use flow identifiers, computed as hashes of specific parts of the packet header, to decide which parallel path a packet takes, and packets with identical hashes are assigned to the same flow and forwarded to the same resource. The presence of a load balancer on the measurement path, and the specific headers and fields used for the forwarding decision, are not known when measuring the path as a black box, so knowledge of the load balancer's flow definition is a prerequisite for repeatable measurements. A path may have more than one stage of load balancing, adding to the complexity.
sections.plainLanguage: Some packets get special treatment in the middle of the network: a certain port, a set priority bits, a label. So a measurement is only meaningful if it says which of those it used, and if it says what changed on the way.

sections.title: What Makes a Packet Standard-Formed
sections.content:
Unless otherwise stated, all metric definitions that concern IP packets include an implicit assumption that the packet is standard-formed. A packet is standard-formed if it meets all of the following required criteria: it includes a valid IP header; it is not an IP fragment; the source and destination addresses correspond to the intended source and destination, including multicast destination addresses; and if a transport header is present, it contains a valid checksum and other valid fields.

For an IPv4 packet to be standard-formed, the additional criteria are that the version field is 4; the Internet Header Length value is at least 5 and the checksum is correct; the total length as given in the IPv4 header corresponds to the size of the IPv4 header plus the size of the payload; the packet possesses either sufficient TTL to travel from the source to the destination if the TTL is decremented by one at each hop, or the maximum TTL of 255; and it does not contain IP options unless explicitly noted.

For an IPv6 packet to be standard-formed, the additional criteria are that the version field is 6; the total length corresponds to the size of the IPv6 header, 40 octets, plus the length of the payload as given in the IPv6 header; the payload length value for the packet, including Extension Headers, conforms to the IPv6 specifications; the packet possesses either sufficient Hop Limit to travel from the source to the destination if the Hop Limit is decremented by one at each hop, or the maximum Hop Limit of 255; the packet either does not contain IP Extension Headers, or it contains the correct number and type of headers as specified in the packet and the headers appear in the standard-conforming order; and all parameters used in the header and Extension Headers are found in the IPv6 parameters registry.

Two mechanisms require discussion: IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Area Networks and Robust Header Compression. The adaptation layer in 6LoWPAN enables the transfer of IPv6 packets over networks with an MTU smaller than the minimum IPv6 MTU, and the fragmentation and reassembly of IPv6 packets, along with the resulting state stored in intermediate nodes, poses substantial challenges to measurements. Likewise, Robust Header Compression operates statefully, compressing headers on subpaths and storing state in intermediate hosts. The modification of measurement packets' Type-P by these mechanisms requires substantial work, as do the requirements for the concept of standard-formed packets, and for these reasons both are considered out of the scope of the standard-formed packet evaluation.

Where IPv6 Extension Headers are present, further considerations apply. Some intermediate nodes may inspect Extension Headers or the entire IPv6 packet while in transit, and in exceptional cases may drop the packet or route via a suboptimal path, so measurements may be unreliable or unrepeatable, although the packet, if it arrives, may be standard-formed with a corresponding Type-P. Some type-length-value options in Hop-by-Hop headers may be permitted to change at intermediate nodes while in transit, again possibly leaving a standard-formed packet with a corresponding Type-P. Although such behaviour is not endorsed by current standards, Extension Headers could be added to or removed from the header chain, and this point simply encourages measurement system designers to be prepared for the unexpected and notify users when such events occur; there are issues with insertion and deletion, such as exceeding the path MTU due to insertion. A change in packet length from the corresponding packet observed at the source, or header modification, is a significant factor in Internet measurement and requires a new Type-P to be reported with the test results.

It is further required that if a packet is described as having a length of B octets, then 0 is at most B and B is at most 65535, and if B is the payload length in octets then B is at most 65535 minus the IP header size in octets, including any Extension Headers. Jumbograms are not covered by that length analysis, but if the IPv6 Jumbogram Payload Hop-by-Hop Option Header is present then a packet with the corresponding length must be considered standard-formed. In practice the path MTU will restrict the length of standard-formed packets that can successfully traverse the path, and Path MTU Discovery or Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery is recommended to prevent fragmentation.

So one might imagine defining an IP-connectivity metric as IP-Type-P-connectivity for standard-formed packets with the IP Diffserv field set to 0, or more succinctly IP-Type-P-connectivity with the IP Diffserv field set to 0, since standard-formed is already implied by convention. Changing the contents of a field, such as the Diffserv Code Point, the ECN bits or the Flow Label may have a profound effect on packet handling during transit but does not affect a packet's status as standard-formed. Likewise, the addition, modification or deletion of extension headers may change the handling of packets in transit hosts.

Finally, RFC 2330 defines the minimal IP packet from A to B as a particular type of standard-formed packet often useful to consider; when defining IP metrics, no packet smaller or simpler than this can be transmitted over a correctly operating IP network. However, the concept has not been employed, since typical active measurement systems employ a transport layer and a payload, and its practical use is limited. The memo therefore deprecates the concept of the minimal IP packet from A to B.
sections.plainLanguage: A standard-formed packet is one that nothing has tampered with: a valid header, the right addresses, no fragments, and any transport header intact. The document writes out the IPv6 version of that checklist, and drops the old rule about the smallest possible packet because nobody used it.

sections.title: Where Translation and NAT Get in the Way
sections.content:
The document adds the key considerations for using IPv6 in two of the IPPM conventions, packets of Type-P and standard-formed packets. The need for coexistence of IPv4 and IPv6 has come from transitioning standards such as the framework for IPv4/IPv6 translation and the IP/ICMP translation algorithms. The definition and execution of measurements within the IPPM framework is challenged whenever such translation mechanisms are present along the measurement path. In use cases like IPv4-IPv6 translation, NAT, protocol encapsulation or IPv6 header compression, the measurement packet's Type-P may be modified along the path, and all these changes must be reported.

The example consequences include the modification or addition of headers or header field values in intermediate nodes, since IPv4-IPv6 transitioning or header compression may change the measurement packets' Type-P, so hosts along the path may treat packets differently because of it, and measurements at observation points along the path may need extra context to uniquely identify a packet.

Network Address Translators on the path can have an unpredictable impact on latency measurement, in terms of the amount of additional time added, and possibly other types of measurements. It is not usually possible to control this impact, as testers may have no control of the underlying network or middleboxes. Stateful NAT may lead to unstable performance for a flow with a specific Type-P, since state has to be created for the first packet of a flow and may be lost later if the NAT runs out of resources. This scenario does not invalidate the Type-P for testing: the purpose of a test might be exactly to quantify the NAT's impact on delay variation. The presence of NAT may mean that the measured performance of a Type-P changes between the source and the destination, which can cause an issue when attempting to correlate measurements conducted on segments of the path that include or exclude the NAT, so it is a factor to be aware of when conducting measurements.

One side effect of the changes made by IPv4-IPv6 transitioning mechanisms is the variable delay that intermediate nodes experience for header modifications. Similar to NAT, the allocation of internal state and establishment of context within intermediate nodes may cause variable delays, depending on the measurement stream pattern and the position of a packet within the stream: the first packet in a stream will typically trigger allocation of internal state in an intermediate transition host, and subsequent packets can benefit from lower processing delay due to the existing state, but large inter-packet delays may result in the intermediate host deleting the associated state and needing to re-establish it on arrival of another packet. This variable delay can itself be an explicit use case for measurements. A further consequence is variable delay due to packet length, because IPv4-IPv6 transitioning or header compression mechanisms modify the length of measurement packets, and the modification of the packet size may or may not change how the measurement path treats the packets.
sections.plainLanguage: A translator in the middle of the path rewrites your test packet, and the rewrite adds time and changes what the packet looks like. The document says report the changes, and notes that the delay from a translator's own bookkeeping is itself something worth measuring.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security considerations that apply to any active measurement of live paths are relevant here as well, and the document points to the one-way and two-way active measurement protocols for them. When considering the privacy of those involved in measurement, or those whose traffic is measured, the sensitive information available to potential observers is greatly reduced when using active techniques that are within the scope of this work. Passive observations of user traffic for measurement purposes raise many privacy issues, and the document refers the reader to the privacy considerations in the LMAP framework, which covers active and passive techniques. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: Measuring with test packets you generate yourself exposes far less than watching everybody's traffic, which is why the framework leans on active measurement. The privacy argument for this is in a separate document.

viz.caption: The additional criteria for a standard-formed packet, by IP version

cells: Internet Header Length value is at least 5, and the checksum is correct.
Fixed at 40 octets, and the total length must match the header plus the payload.
Enough TTL to reach the destination, or the maximum of 255.
Enough Hop Limit to reach the destination, or the maximum of 255.
No IP options, unless explicitly noted.
Either no Extension Headers, or the correct number and type in the standard-conforming order, with all parameters from the IPv6 parameters registry.

viz.caption: Packet characteristics that a measurement has to state

items.title: IP header fields and values
items.text: The version, the addresses, the length, the priority bits and the hop counter.

items.title: Transport port numbers
items.text: Whether the packets are for well-known TCP ports, unreserved UDP ports, or something else.

items.title: Higher-layer headers
items.text: The headers and values of the protocol carried in the packet.

items.title: Diffserv and ECN
items.text: The differentiated services code point and the congestion notification bits.

items.title: Router Alert and Flow Label
items.text: Header fields that can cause a router to treat a packet specially.

items.title: Hop-by-Hop extensions
items.text: Options that intermediate nodes may inspect or change.

items.title: Extension header count and order
items.text: How many extension headers there are and that they are in the standard order.

items.title: Checksum validity
items.text: Whether the IPv4 checksum and any transport checksum are correct.

viz.caption: The effects of translation on a measurement

items.title: Headers get rewritten
items.text: Translating or compressing changes the Type-P, so hosts on the path may treat the packet differently and observation points may need more context to identify it.

items.title: NAT adds unpredictable delay
items.text: The amount of extra time a NAT adds is not controllable, and stateful NAT may lose the state for a flow and have to recreate it.

items.title: Internal state causes variable delay
items.text: The first packet of a stream triggers state allocation in a transition host and is slower than the ones that follow; a long gap can make it delete the state and start again.

items.title: Packet length changes
items.text: Translation and compression change the size of the packet, which may or may not change how the path treats it.
